newsitem.title: CYPRUS: U.N. invites Cypriot leaders to July 9 talks.
newsitem.headline: U.N. invites Cypriot leaders to July 9 talks.

text.p: Leaders of Cyprus's Greek and Turkish communities will meet in New York on July 9 in their first encounter for nearly three years to try to break the deadlock in the long-standing dispute splitting the island, the United Nations said on Wednesday.

Both sides have accepted an invitation from U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan to come to talks at a New York location between July 9 and 13, ending months of shuttle diplomacy in preparation for the meeting.

Gustave Feissel, the Secretary-General's permanent representative on the island, confirmed that he had handed Annan's invitation to Cypriot President Glafcos Clerides and later to Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash.

The two leaders, who have not met in nearly three years, both said they would accept the invitations, although the Greek Cypriot side has expressed concern that the Turkish Cypriot side has not shifted its position on the protracted dispute which could open a window of optimism.
Clerides, the leader of the Greek Cypriot community, told reporters the talks would start on July 9 and end on July 13 at a location close to New York.
"They (the United Nations) have not decided where they will take place," said Clerides. "We will find out in a few days."
On the other side of the barbed wire slicing through the island, Denktash said he would go to the meeting with goodwill, and to defend the rights of the Turkish Cypriot community.
"This meeting is not aimed at reaching an immediate solution, but it is a beginning. We hope it will be a new beginning with a new spirit," he said after meeting Feissel.

"We hope that the Greek Cypriot side comes with a positive approach, giving up its intention of continuing to usurp our rights under false title of the government of Cyprus, accepting the concept of bi-zonality and the exchange of properties as necessitated by bi-zonality," said Denktash.
Greek Cypriot officials said Annan would host a dinner for the two leaders on July 8, the eve of the talks.

"The start of the talks will be chaired by the United Nations Secretary-General and he will later hand things over to his representative, Diego Cordovez," said Cypriot government spokesman Manolis Christofides.
Annan appointed Cordovez, a former foreign minister of Ecuador and ex U.N. under-secretary general, as his special adviser on Cyprus earlier this year.

Last week U.S. President Bill Clinton appointed Richard Holbrooke, negotiator of the 1995 Bosnia peace accord, as special emissary for the eastern Mediterranean island, which has been divided since a Turkish invasion of its north in 1974.
The talks come against a backdrop of increased concern at the risks of militarisation of the island, and membership talks between Cyprus and the European Union next year.

Turkish forces seized northern Cyprus in July 1974 in response to a brief Greek Cypriot coup engineered by the military then ruling Greece. Some 30,000 mainland Turkish soldiers are stationed in northern Cyprus. The south has a defence pact with Greece, its closest ally and a NATO member.
Clerides's Greek Cypriot-led government is recognised internationally while Denktash heads a breakaway Turkish Cypriot state declared in 1983 and recognised only by Ankara.
A government comprising both Greek and Turkish Cypriots formed after independence from Britain in 1960 broke down in 1963.
